Distinguished Head of State and Government, distinguished Ministers, distinguished representatives of observers, entities of the United Nations system and other accredited intergovernmental organizations, representatives of civil society, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I call to order the fourth multi-stakeholder roundtable of the fourth International Conference on Financing for Development on the theme, Upholding the Multilateral Trading System and Harnessing the Potential of Science, Technology and Innovation. Let me take this opportunity to cordially welcome all of you to this multi-stakeholder roundtable. I'm honored to serve you as your co-chair together with Her Excellency Melita Gabric, Deputy Minister of Foreign and European Affairs and Minister for Development of Slovenia. The summary of our discussion here today will be presented to the closing plenary meeting of the conference in the afternoon of Thursday, 3 July, and included in the final report of the conference. Before we proceed, I would like to make some introductory remarks about the theme of our discussion today. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honour to co-chair this important roundtable on a topic that lies at the very heart of our shared ambitions building a resilient, fair and inclusive global economy through effective multilateralism and forward-looking innovation. We are meeting at a time of profound global disruption, marked by increasing geopolitical tension, economic fragmentation and widening inequalities. all while humanity faces an accelerating twin transition, digital and ecological. In this context, preserving and strengthening the multilateral trading system is not just desirable, it is indispensable. A rules-based transparent and inclusive trade framework remains the most powerful driver of sustainable growth and global cooperation. But the system must evolve. As highlighted in the CV outcome document, the reform of the WTO is essential not only to restore trust and efficiency, but to ensure that the voices and needs of developing countries and least developed countries are fully reflected. This includes reaffirming the principle of special and differential treatment and accelerating the full implementation of the Trade Facilitation Agreement. Morocco remains firmly committed to these goals. Since May of this year, we have fully implemented the agreement, simplifying trade procedures and reinforcing our role as a regional logistics and trade hub. We also grant duty-free access to products from African LDCs, fostering deeper integration into regional and global value chains. Ladies and gentlemen, trade alone is not enough. To make development truly inclusive, we must leverage the power of science, technology and innovation, but we must do so responsibly. We cannot ignore the risks. Without deliberate action, innovation may deepen divides rather than bridge them. This is why bridging the digital divide must be a shared priority. Morocco's digital strategy 2030 reflects this vision. We are investing in broadband access in rural and remote areas, equipping youth and women with digital skills, and promoting inclusive fintech to improve access to financial services for vulnerable population. Tools like mobile payment, digital microcredit, and microinsurance are helping to reduce disparities and expand opportunities. But technology must be governed. We must promote digital sovereignty, robust data protection, and the prevention of misuse, especially as AI and emerging technology reshape our societies. The goal is clear. Technology must be a tool for social justice and shared progress, not a new form of exclusion. Finally, promoting structural transformation in the Global South requires local value creation. Morocco has made a strategic choice to invest in the sustainable development of natural resources, particularly through green hydrogen, phosphate-based fertilizers, and clean industrial ecosystem in sectors like automotive, aerospace, electronics, and renewable energy. These efforts are aligned with the SEVIE outcome documents call for development models based on sustainability, local added value, and regional integration. Distinguished delegates, this roundtable offers a timely opportunity to reaffirm our collective responsibility to ensure that trade, technology and innovation become genuine enablers for sustainable development, not privileges reserved for the few. Let us work together with ambition and urgency to build a more inclusive, balanced and resilient global economy. Thank you. I now invite my fellow co-chair, Her Excellency Melita Gabric, Deputy Minister for Foreign and European Affairs and Minister for Development of Slovenia, to make some opening remarks.

I thank my fellow co-chair, Your Excellency Nadia Fetta, Minister of Economy and Finance of Morocco, and will proceed to deliver my opening remarks. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, I am honored and pleased to have this opportunity to chair the roundtable. Rapid advances in STI create enormous potential for accelerating the achievement of the SDGs. They play a critical role in shaping global trade by enhancing productivity, creating new industries, and increasing efficiency of global supply chains. However, these benefits are not distributed equally and may even deepen divides by leading to unintended economic, environmental, and social impacts. We must therefore ensure that advances in SDI are inclusive, equitable, and accessible to all. To this end, Slovenia attaches great importance to finding solutions that include youth, women and older persons, thereby ensuring that no one is left behind. In recent years, Slovenia has considerably increased investments in science, technology and innovation. We recognize and stress the importance of international partnerships to fully develop their potential and to avoid negative societal and environmental impacts. Since 2020, Slovenia hosts the International Research Center in Artificial Intelligence, which operates under the auspices of UNESCO. Together with its partners, the center develops open access AI solutions, that are applicable to achieving the sustainable development goals. One such solution to mention is the Water Observatory, which represents Slovenia's commitment and contribution to the UN Water Action Agenda. The Slovenian Center of Excellence for Space Science and Technologies, SpaceSI, is working with satellite data and digital models of ecosystems to build resilience against climate change. In 2023, Space SI joined the global initiative, Twinning of Rivers, led by Ganga Center for Ganga River Basin Management and Studies. Space SI is also engaged in using satellite and digital technologies for management of river basins in Kenya. We pay special attention to cooperation with local universities and companies, to transfer knowledge and to build capacities of our local partners. A good example of interregional cooperation is the Digital for Development Hub, which is a part of the overall Global Gateway strategy, the EU's foremost initiative to boost investments in partner countries. Slovenia is particularly committed to its operation in Latin America and the Caribbean, where we put a special focus on AI. I look forward to a dynamic exchange of views on how to utilize the commitments adopted here in Seville to strengthen the multilateral trading system and leverage the power of science, technology and innovation for promoting shared prosperity. Thank you.

I thank my fellow co-chair for these remarks. We shall now hear a special address. I have the great honour to invite His Excellency Pedro Sanchez, President of the Government of Spain, to address the round table.

Ministers, your Excellencies, This Seville conference is addressing crucial challenges such as financing for development, international cooperation, debt and international taxation. Of course, these are all urgent, important issues because the figures speak crystal clear. The world needs to mobilize $4 trillion per year to achieve the sustainable development goals. 3.4 billion people in the world live in nations whose governments spend more on paying debt interest than in investing in health and education put together. This is a reality that is not just unjust but also unacceptable. Of course, we're not here to surrender. We're here to show that it's possible to make progress, that there are solutions. I also think It's important to say that history confirms that over the last 50 years, life expectancy has gone up by 14 years, GDP per capita in the world has more than doubled, and a cell phone has more calculating power than the most powerful computer 50 years ago. So there has been outstanding progress. in trade, science, and also in cooperation. These are the three pillars of success, and they can only be fully realized in open societies. However, this engine for development is struggling today. We have to recognize this. We're speaking about tariffs, trade wars, and this is not just rhetoric. If we look at the figures, it seems that global growth will go down by 3% as a result of some of these policies. So who is paying the price for this? Of course, as always, the most vulnerable are going to bear the brunt. Tariffs are not a useful weapon. They are a break on progress. Unfair competition, of course, is a problem, but if we respond with barriers, then we will all lose. There are no winners in such a trade war. That is why I agree with the chair that it is urgent that we reform the international system. We must reaffirm the crucial role of the World Trade Organization, and we should also recognize that today's world has little in common with the world that existed when GATT was established in 1995 and even has changed a lot in the last 10 years. We're talking about investment and how that will be channeled into the economy in an increasingly digital economy. Of course, we need to adapt the rules, and that is the challenge that we have ahead of us. We've also seen geopolitical changes. A diplomatic country cannot -- a developing country can't be an eternal category. We need to look at the relevance of these terms. The rules need to reflect the world as it is today and not as it was. and it must inspire us to build the world that we want. That is why we need to have know-how. Without shared know-how, there can be no way of moving forward. Without technical cooperation, we won't be able to move forward either. And without cooperation, we won't be able to have a sustainable future. If we just resign ourselves to isolation, we will all lose out. I would like to make Spain's position on these issues quite clear. We have very clear priorities. First of all, we believe in open science. Knowledge cannot be a privilege. This is something we push forward at the national and international level. We are convinced that sharing knowledge is the only way to address global challenges. Second, equality and inclusion. because we have often excluded many people, including women, from decision-making positions. Are we really going to do the same in the future, for instance, excluding indigenous populations and local communities from the future? And finally, we need to have equitable access because many countries are not just facing barriers to innovate, but also to access the know-how that others generate. And I think that is a gap that only multiplies inequalities. We are in favor of a fair chain of innovation all the way through the process. We're not just talking about principles here, we're also talking about facts. We are leading forward an initiative with 18 other countries to focus on research, for instance, in sustainable agriculture. Science is at the service of life and also for sustainable development. Trade, science and cooperation are all the keys and they're not just abstract concepts, they are instruments of progress and they're also factors of justice. Development will not be genuine if it's not shared and that's what we have to do, we need to expand development to all areas of all societies. It can only be lasting and sustainable if it is based on clear, fair rules. Spain is committed. We are defending the rules and we are advocating working together to achieve the future that we want. Thank you so much.

I thank the President of the Government of Spain. I'm also pleased to welcome the distinguished presenter of this discussion. I also welcome Mr. Jorge Moreira da Silva, Executive Director of the United Nations Office for Project Services, who will moderate the discussion. I now turn the meeting over to the moderator. I look forward to an open, constructive, and productive exchange of views.

Thank you very much, distinguished co-chairs, excellencies, delegates. It's an honor to join you today to moderate this session and ahead of giving the floor to the panelists, I'd like to provide two, three minutes quick remarks. Ten years ago in Addis Ababa, countries recognized that public finance alone through ODA and domestic resource mobilization wouldn't be sufficient. They called for mobilization of public and private finance to meet the trillions needed to achieve SDGs and the climate goals. And crucially, they called as well for improved global trade. Since then, despite some progress, critical bottlenecks have held us back. Insufficient capacity to implement at national and local levels. Finance flows misaligned from the SDGs, finance flowing often to the easiest context and not where it's most needed, especially in LDCs, conflict and fragile context. And the new development finance landscape has emerged, but the development finance architecture has not caught up. Our ways of doing things are still outdated and fragmented. Both Addis and Seville rightly emphasise that international trade is an engine for sustainable development. Yet, the multilateral trading system is facing significant headwinds. We are seeing a worldwide increase in trade restrictions, including tariffs that are inconsistent with WTO agreements. This is a concerning trend. made worse by rising trade tensions and the lack of progress in multilateral negotiations. Developing countries are struggling to integrate into regional and global value chains. LDCs, LLDCs, SEEDS and many middle-income countries can miss out due to restricted productive capacities and inadequate trade infrastructure. We need urgent and concrete steps to address this. We need scaled-up and more equitable financing. The Seville document is clear in its vision. It reaffirms the centrality of a rules-based inclusive multilateral trading system. And it calls for bold steps to close digital divides and build on scientific and technological advances to improve trade capacities. to better integrate countries into regional and global value chains, to help countries get more out of their commodities and critical minerals and move value chains, and to promote digital solutions to bridge gaps. But let's not forget, as we speak in this AI era, that one third of the population is still offline. Advancing measures It's a collective responsibility and of course, UNOPS within our mandate on implementation, on infrastructure procurement and project management, we are also committed to do so. Let me now move to the panelists. It's indeed a pleasure to moderate this high level panel. We have a distinguished group of speakers with us today and I know that we are all eager to hear their insights. Before we begin, a quick note on timekeeping and apologies for the panelists, but I really need to be strict on the timekeeping. Each panelist will have five minutes. This will help us ensure we have time for discussion and engagement following your presentations. Let me introduce our first panelist. I'm pleased to welcome His Excellency Mr. Shane Reti, Minister for Science and Innovation, Minister for Pacific Peoples, Minister for Statistics and Universities of New Zealand. Minister, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Mr. Moderator. Greetings to everyone. Greetings to dignitaries and to colleagues and panellists to either side of me. Thank you for the opportunity to speak on behalf of the New Zealand Government about how we can uphold the multilateral trading system and build capacity in science, technology and innovation in developing countries. Recognising the fellow panellists and some of the insights we've already heard, two particular points that the President raised resonate with me. He said, "Lasting and sustainable trade needs clear, fair rules." And, "Trade, science, and cooperation are factors of progress." I'd like to tackle the trade aspect of this session first. The international trade architecture that has been in place since the end of World War II has contributed to creating economic conditions that have lifted millions out of poverty globally. It has also helped New Zealand to remain a competitive exporter despite our size and geographic remoteness. But the stability provided by the international trade system is no longer guaranteed. The growing disregard for international trading rules and norms is bad for everybody, and has outsized impacts on developing and trade-dependent economies. New Zealand's most important trade priority is to uphold the multilateral trading system, with the World Trade Organisation at its core. We must push back against the use and threat of trade measures that are outside the agreed rules, including trade tariffs, non-tariff barriers, and trade-distorting subsidies. Through the WTO and regional free trade agreements, New Zealand will advocate for appropriately sequenced and paced trade liberalisation that opens up markets for developing country exporters. Through our international development cooperation, we will continue to support businesses in developing countries, particularly in sectors like agriculture, to move beyond commodity production to produce higher quality products and services, such as well-branded food products that attract higher prices. I will turn now to science, technology and innovation. New Zealand is very supportive of the corresponding chapter of the Compromisso de Sevilla. We must take steps to address the digital divide and support all countries to harness the full potential of technology. In particular, we see digital technologies as a critical enabler, particularly in small island developing states in the Pacific, helping them to overcome the challenges posed by small size and geographic remoteness. This is expressed in the Compromisso de Sevilla as supporting CIDS, Centres of Excellence in Innovation and Technology, as a mechanism to provide capacity building, learning opportunities, exchange experiences and support innovation in CIDS. New Zealand will continue to support developing countries to close the digital divide. In the Pacific we support both the development of core infrastructure, for example laying undersea cables and domestic fibre networks, and initiatives that strengthen local capacity to manage them. The education system has a critical role to play in improving capacity in science and technology. In the compromesso document, this is described with ambitions towards building the science, innovation and technology workforce of the future with scholarships for developing countries, cultural and academic exchanges for students in STEM fields, and promotion of vocational education, training and skills in STEM subjects, including through public-private partnerships and engagements with industry. New Zealand addresses this ambition with core support to educational institutes in partner countries. In these places, we are assisting professionals in the adult workforce in upskilling in new technologies and artificial intelligence. For example, through our partnership with the Commonwealth of Learning, we are supporting women to learn about technology, enhancing employability, fostering entrepreneurship, and cultivating digital leadership within their communities. As an emerging technology along with innovative use of data, the Compromiso de Sevilla promotes equitable and inclusive access to and development of artificial intelligence, along with leveraging non-traditional data sources such as administrative records, geospatial information, mobile data, citizen-generated data, and remote sensing. We should remember that science, technology, and innovation are not just about the internet and digital services. Farmers, business, and tour operators and processes also need access to scientific research and technology. They need to be innovative in the way they reach international consumers and meet the increasing demands for traceability and sustainability. They need to effectively adapt to the adverse impacts of climate change. New Zealand offers a range of support to build scientific and innovation capacity in developing countries and with a focus on the Pacific and Southeast Asia. We take a practical approach to scientific research with particular strengths in agriculture. We also work to improve adoption of digital technology and services among specific businesses to improve their competitiveness and links to customers in international markets. To conclude, I thank you once again for this opportunity to contribute to this discussion about strengthening the multilateral trading system and harnessing the potential of science, technology and innovation, and I look forward to further insights and dialogue. Thank you, Mr. Moderator.

Thank you, Minister, and thank you for respecting the five minutes. Next, I'm honored to hear from His Excellency, Mr. Karamoko Jean-Marie Traore, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Regional Cooperation and Burkina Abroad of Burkina Faso. Excellency, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Chair. I'm very honored to be able to take part in this roundtable. which focuses on two essential pillars of sustainable development, a more equitable multilateral trading system and the strategic role of science, technology and innovation. For Burkina Faso, these are not abstract issues. They are part of our national ambition to achieve a structural transformation of our economy in the context of complex challenges, but with major opportunities as well. Supporting the multilateral trading system is a matter of justice in our eyes. In addition to being a matter of justice, it is an existential question for us as well, because it is one of the safest ways for us to allow the most vulnerable people to access the international trading system. That is why we think it is so important that we work hand in hand, in solidarity with other countries who have similar realities to ours, to ensure that our international trading system can play its proper role, facilitating trade but also upholding the rights of countries who are in an unfavourable position from the start. In Burkina Faso we have a large cotton industry. People working in the cotton industry work extremely hard but they are often victims to subsidies that do not allow them to fully profit from their product. And the same goes for producers of coffee in our country as well. And that is why it's so important that we have a fair, effective international trading system that can allow us to protect the rights of our producers. I think we should come back to the role of international cooperation, which I think is particularly important if we are to have appropriate guidelines in this area. We need to have a mutual understanding of the realities that countries are facing. Trade is a tool of communication and inclusion. It can be used to carry out broad change in societies and that is why it is such an important lever for development in our countries. If we look at the issue of technology, I think it's an opportunity for us to have additional means through technology to allow producers to first of all access information, of course. In our country we have farmers who are in far-flung areas of our country who don't have a lot of information but now thanks to technology they are able to be informed about important issues for their businesses and for instance very accurate weather forecasts much more than before so access to technology is very important for them. And then they can also have access to information about tariffs and prices in the markets. This allows people to have to make fully informed decisions because they are fully informed about what the relevant prices are that are being set in their markets. So these are such important innovative tools that we're seeing developed. So it allows them ultimately to be more competitive on global markets by having access to all of this information. We think Seville, represents a great opportunity for us to rethink the development model, to look at what we've achieved, but also to see at some of the shortcomings that we have seen in the tools that we've used up to now. Of course, it's important to respect the spirit of the SDGs, but we also need to look at what is happening on the ground and adjust our answers and responses accordingly. Seville represents an opportunity for us. It is an opportunity for us to have a fresh start, to rethink how we do business. I would just like to conclude by saying that we fully support the document that has been adopted, which will allow us at least to have a guide to show us the way forward as we do our best to achieve our shared goals. Thank you for your attention.

Thank you very much, Minister, and thank you for respecting the speaking time.

Mr. Philippe Gock, Secretary of Economic and Financial Affairs from Brazil.

Thank you, moderator, co-chairs, fellow colleagues of the panel. This roundtable is divided into two broad topics, multilateral trading system and science and technology. Given the limited time that we have, I'll focus my comments on the first part, on the multilateral trading system, specifically what we can jointly do in order to reinforce the WTO in these challenging times. This discussion is very timely as we are a few months away from MC14 in Cameroon in which we'll have to take some tough decisions there and it's important for us to expedite our discussions here. Let's speak a bit about the context of what we are try to look into here. The WTO, as we all know, is facing an existential crisis and it's affecting its functionality. You can maybe trace back the problem to July 2008 when we had that big impasse in the Doha round, but things only got worse and since then and it's accelerating, the problems are accelerating since then. We have seen many countries taking measures that would be questionable according to the parameters of some important texts of the GATT, WTO such as TRIMS, industrial subsidies and others and more recently even Some basic principles of the WTO or from the old GATT, 1947, have also been questioned. For instance, most favored nation and bound rates and so on. So we have a situation that's really challenging, not to mention the situation in the dispute settlement mechanism, which is also difficult. So we see unilateral and protectionist measures, sometimes disguised as measures related to green transition and industry protection, all of this in the context of a new digital economy. So all this compounds to exacerbate the asymmetries in the system to the detriment of the interest of basically developing countries. We are in the worst possible scenario. We still have the rules there that in many cases they limit our policy space, but we have to respect them and others are not doing that or at least not doing it in full or selectively disrespecting. This gives rise to a growing sense of frustration, especially in developing countries, and we lose the predictability of the system. So what to do about this situation? The main message is that inaction is not an option. We have, as others have said here before, think of a serious reform of the WTO. There is a growing recognition about that, although we might have some divergences still about how deep this reform should be and at what pace. Brazil, we think that we should tackle both questions of substance and of process in this discussion. And we should arrive at the point in which we get to a WTO, a new WTO that's much more flexible and transparent. These should be the key characteristics, in our opinion, of this renewed WTO. Of course, looking into very carefully of how the new dispute settlement mechanism should function. We are in Brazil preparing some proposals that we could circulate as soon as possible. We would have to take into account a scenario in which we have some characteristics that are completely different from the '90s. We have the borders between trading goods and services, they are not very clear anymore in many cases. We have to tackle environmental unilateral measures. We have to make sure that the benefits of science and technology, they are spread to developing countries. And in all, we have to make sure that we operate in a scenario in which the WTO has a true development approach. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Minister. Now I'm very pleased finally to give the floor to His Excellency Ambassador Enrique Ochoa Martinez, is Under Secretary for Multilateral Affairs and Human Rights at the Government of Mexico. Ambassador.

Thank you very much, moderator, Your Excellencies, dear colleagues. This conference is being held at a defining moment. The convergence between trade, science, technology and innovation can be a turning point for sustainable development, or it could deepen existing structural inequalities. We welcome that the outcome document clearly shows that trade and technology can be used to achieve sustainable development and it recognizes the urgent need to revitalize the world trading system. It also stresses the need to foster scientific and technological cooperation and to close digital gaps focusing on equality and sovereignty. We fully agree with the appeal to boost responsible innovation, to reject protectionism, and to strengthen open, inclusive, and rules-based international trade. Mexico believes that international trade should be built on clear, predictable, and fair rules geared towards facilitating productive diversification, economic resilience, and social inclusion. We will promote the full implementation of the Trade Facilitation Agreement and also binding clauses on sustainability, gender equality, labor rights, and regional development in trade agreements. We are in favor of a revitalized WTO with a strengthened deliberative function and a forum for the priorities that the global south has. We also think that access to know how and knowledge should be a global public good. International cooperation should facilitate technology transfer, open science and capacity building in the domains of research, innovation and digital infrastructure. Mexico promotes training talent in key sectors such as AI, data analysis, automation and cybersecurity. without overlooking the importance of keeping our languages, our traditional knowledge and our traditional know-how and vocations. We are in favor of people-centered innovation with ethical digital governance, public investment in technical education and significant meaningful connectivity, upholding people's rights and achieving tangible results. We're also in favor of the establishment of multilateral standards for data governance, responsible algorithms, and interoperable platforms. We agree that emerging technologies need appropriate public policy with the cooperation of all and multi-stakeholder governance. That is why we're in favor of a link between this agenda and the Global Digital Compact. focusing on consistency between the two and intergenerational justice. We believe that trade and technology are not neutral, they reflect the kind of development that we want to build. Only with a human rights approach, focusing on economic justice and multinational cooperation, can we turn them into genuine catalysts for shared prosperity and sustainable resilience. Thank you.

Thank you so much.

For respecting the time. I know it's difficult, but I think it was amazing the way that it has been provided by the panelists. Now, I would like to turn to our two lead discussants. I kindly ask the lead discussants to provide their comments within three minutes. I will start by welcoming Mr. Ian Sanders, Secretary General of the Customs Cooperation Council. The floor is yours.

Thank you, moderator. As a global voice of customs representing 186 member administrations, the Customs Cooperation Council or World Customs Organization recognizes the importance of increasing predictability, efficiency, and resilience in the global trading system, as doing so reduces frictions at borders, increases accessibility for more companies, and creates jobs. Results also include more accurate revenue collection, key to domestic resource mobilization, This combination of stability and transparency are particularly critical to developing countries and landlocked developing countries. The WCO maintains instruments, including two that form part of our initiative in the Seville Platform of Action, that when applied by members, build trust at critical points along global supply chains. In the case of the International Convention on Simplification and Harmonization of Customs Procedures, or the revised Kyoto Convention, the principles are clearly stated. Simplicity in procedures combined with effective risk management create the best environment for legitimate trade. And these ideas also appear in the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement. The harmonized system standardizes the classification rules for thousands of commodities for its 200 users. Its widespread application enables goods to be consistently classified worldwide. Additionally, the HS supports accurate trade statistics that can inform governments as they develop their trade policies. The WCO not only maintains standards that support international trade, it supports members that strive to implement them. We know the effect of standards is realized through implementation, and my organization works around the world to this end. as it is essential to members' effective integration into the rules-based multilateral trading system. The revised Kyoto Convention and the HS guide efficient and effective procedure, but in a trade environment marked by high volume, complexity and expectations, the WCO looks to technology and innovation to optimize their effect. Our members do not start at the same place technologically, so we help customs administrations transform concepts into real-world practice Whenever development partners enable us to do so. When successful, single windows enable traders to submit data one time. The WCO data model is used for cross-border data exchange. Automated risk management supports customs clearance decisions even before goods arrive. And most importantly, traders know the rules and how to comply. Still, we know much more needs to be done. So the WCO is committed to an environment that facilitates legitimate trade, and supports economic development, we stand ready to continue the support of our members and the multilateral trading system. Thank you.
Thank you very much, Mr. Sanders. Now I'd like to give the floor to Ms. Randal Sengupta from the Third World Network, also part of the civil society FFD mechanism. Ms. Sengupta. The floor is yours.

Thank you, Mr. Moderator. Trade and investment policy, if designed right, can contribute immensely to sustainable development, but seems to have lost its way in the multilateral trading system. The current turbulence and uncertainty is impacting all countries, but developing countries and LDCs remain much more vulnerable. And as President Sanchez just said, with greater impact on vulnerable constituencies, including women, indigenous peoples, the poor, small farmers, workers, patients, others as all our countries are forced to make trade deals spanning a number of areas in addition to tariffs. This only reaffirms how fragile and inequitable the multilateral trading system has already been and how the talk of delivering on development has been rather rhetorical. Coming at this critical moment, I agree with Minister Traore from Burkina Faso that FFD4 under the aegis of the UN had the potential to lay the pathway for bold and ambitious reshaping of the global trading system. Unfortunately, in spite of a promising start, the negotiations saw a gradual weakening of ambition and the inability to deliver much concrete actions on some critical areas, some of which I really want to highlight. First, environmental related trade measures, especially unilateral ones, are unfair, especially when not underpinned by the principle of CBDR. They give rise to concerns that these are aimed at securing commercial advantages and not sustainability, and threaten to cut out producers in the global south, especially small farmers, fishers and SMEs from production and trade opportunities. The FFD4 outcome document provides for discussion but does not address the issue adequately as there are no actions planned after such a discussion. The second area where we had much expectation is with regard to the investor state dispute settlement mechanism. This provision has led to compensation paid to MNCs totaling something like 114 billion US dollars have massively undermined government's policy space, both in the global north and in the global south to pursue sustainable development objectives. For example, measures related to climate action, natural resource conservation, health, tax, labor policies and the rights of communities have all been threatened. Reform of the ISDS is already underway as UNCITRAL, but has major weaknesses. There was realistic scope for Member States at FFD4 to go beyond reform and decisively agree to secede from such provisions across all investment agreements and implement a standstill on all ISDS cases until then. However, this did not happen. Going forward, we sincerely hope Member States will engage in designing an effective reform process with immediate effect and will agree to a standstill until that is completed. Third, the outcome document prompts developing countries and LDCs to fully liberalize e-commerce. Estimates show that they are already going to lose US$26 billion in tariff revenues on e-transmissions in 2025. Moreover, digital policymaking is a critical area for them and trade policy must preserve future national policy space, as Minister Feta from Morocco already pointed out, in particular for retaining ownership and control over national data, which is key raw material for future development, for nationally suited and beneficial digital industrialization policies, for addressing digital infrastructure development and digital divide, and the right to regulate activities of global digital corporations, the right to tax them. Finally, critical minerals is an area of concern. We understand the interest in attracting investment in this sector, but it's also imperative that developing countries and LDCs retain the policy space to ensure local value addition, beneficiation for structural transformation. So they must have full policy flexibility over their trade and investment policies. So let me end by saying the FFD4 outcome document has fallen short on delivering on an ambitious trade agenda. We had hoped for more specific tools, but we do hope future actions will fill this deficit. We as civil society look forward to play our legitimate participatory role and to engage actively with all of you on this area. Thank you so much.

Thank you very much, Ms. Sengupta. I would like to thank all the panelists and lead discussions for their inspiring remarks. Now, I would like to pass the floor back to our co-chairs who will lead the next phase of the interactive dialogue. Thank you.

I thank Mr. Moreira da Silva for expertly guiding the discussion.
